the-secret:
The Secret by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Two nude lovers press together on a rough bronze rock — his hand braced on the stone, her arm around his neck, their mouths joined in a kiss held at intimate scale.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A man leans forward from the left, his back arched and one hand planted on the craggy base. A woman sits against the rock to his right, head lifted to meet him, her arm reaching around his neck to draw him down. Their lips touch at the centre of the group. Rodin leaves the faces slightly softened — less portrait than gesture — but the bodies read clearly: shoulder, spine, thigh, the weight of one figure settling into the other. The bronze carries a dark brown patina with green in the hollows of the rock and along the spine. Light slides across the polished ridges of muscle and catches in the tool-marked skin.

Rodin conceived the group around 1894. This cast was made in 1960 at the Georges Rudier foundry in Paris under licence from the Musée Rodin — signed, stamped with the founder's mark, and marked with the museum copyright on the base. At twenty-seven point nine centimetres it is deliberately small: an embrace you approach at close range rather than from across a gallery.

Walk around it slowly. From behind you see the man's strained back and the woman's curved spine; from the front, the closed circuit of their arms; from the side, the narrow space where the kiss actually happens. The title asks you to read privacy into what is, on the surface, an open display of tenderness.
main-crispee-droite:
Large Clenched Right Hand by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
An isolated right hand enlarged to monumental scale — fingers twisted in a grip that reads as strain, defiance, or inner turmoil, drawn from the expressive vocabulary of The Gates of Hell.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A single right hand rises from a rough integral base, severed at the wrist. The fingers curl in a tense, twisted grip — not a closed fist but a clutch that strains outward, thumb extended. Knuckles, tendons, and the heel of the palm are modelled at nearly half-metre scale, every tool mark visible. Dark bronze patina pools green in the recesses between the fingers.

Rodin isolated and enlarged this hand as an autonomous study drawn from The Gates of Hell. The grand modèle lets the wrist and forearm stump read as monumental fragments in their own right.

This example was cast at the Georges Rudier foundry in Paris in 1962 under licence from the Musée Rodin, signed on the exterior with an interior stamp confirming the museum-sanctioned edition.
age-of-bronze-small:
The Age of Bronze by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Rodin's first major success in reduction — the iconic pose of one hand on the head, the other lifted, preserved at a scale suited to intimate display.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A dark-patinated bronze man stands with his right hand on top of his head and his left arm lowered at his side. His head tilts back; eyes are heavy, almost closed. Weight settles on one leg; the chest and shoulders are modelled with anatomical precision at sixty-four centimetres — the second reduction of Rodin's first great nude.

L'Âge d'Airain stunned the Paris Salon of 1877 with its realism; Rodin was briefly accused of casting from life. The model was Auguste Neyt, a young Belgian soldier.

This bronze was cast in October 1945 at the Alexis Rudier foundry in Paris, with the founder's mark at the back and Rodin's signature on the base.
age-of-bronze:
The Age of Bronze by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A life-size male nude, one hand on his head, the other raised — Rodin's first independent masterpiece, so disconcertingly real that the Paris Salon accused him of casting it directly from the body.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A life-size bronze man stands with his right arm raised high above his head and his left forearm held near his shoulder. His head falls back; eyes are closed or lifted toward the ceiling. Weathered green-black patina covers the chest, ribs, and abdomen, catching light along the collarbones and the raised arm. The pose is alert yet suspended — as if waking, or remembering.

Rodin began the figure in October 1875 in Brussels, after returning from Italy and his first encounter with Michelangelo. His model was Auguste Neyt, a young Belgian soldier. Neyt later remembered standing for hours while Rodin shifted the pose by inches.

Originally the figure held a long spear in his left hand, and Rodin titled him Le Vaincu — The Vanquished — in memory of the defeated French. Then he removed the spear. With the weapon gone, the gesture became unreadable: is the man waking up, dying, dreaming, lifting himself out of nothing? Rodin renamed him The Age of Bronze after Hesiod's Third Age of Man, and the ambiguity stuck. He stands halfway between sleep and consciousness, halfway between idealised classical nude and something startlingly modern.

When the plaster reached the Salons of Brussels and Paris in 1877, critics accused Rodin of casting from life. A group of his peers — Falguière, Carrier-Belleuse, Dubois — finally signed a public defence. The State bought the plaster and commissioned this, the first bronze, from Thiébaut Frères in 1880. Rodin was awarded a third-class medal at the Salon. He never made a life-size figure again. He had already learned what he needed.
danaide:
Danaïde by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A woman kneels face-down on a rough bronze rock, back arched, hair pouring forward over the stone — punishment made visible in the body alone.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

She is folded into herself on a craggy base: knees drawn under, hips raised, face hidden against her arm. Long hair spills down the rock face in thick bronze strands that merge with the texture of the stone beneath her. The back and shoulders catch the light; the hollows along the spine and beneath the folded limbs hold shadow and green patina. There is no jar, no other figure — only this compact, muscular body given over to weight and exhaustion. Rodin's signature sits on the side of the base.

In Greek myth the Danaïdes were condemned to draw water forever in vessels that could not hold it. Rodin modelled one of them around 1885 for The Gates of Hell, then let her stand alone, as he did with so many figures lifted out of that monumental swarm. This Arkın cast is bronze with a rich dark brown and red-brown patination — not the famous white marble in Paris, but the same pose preserved at twenty-one centimetres.

Move around the base. From above you read the arc of the spine; from the side, the raised curve of the hip and the pour of hair; from behind, the shoulders braced as if still carrying something you cannot see. The punishment lives in the posture, not in any attribute Rodin chose to leave out.
je-suis-belle:
I Am Beautiful by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Two figures locked in a close bronze embrace — her head thrown back, his face at her breast, the title drawn from Baudelaire.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Seen at close range, the group is all leaning bodies and interlocked limbs. A man bends down over a woman whose head falls back, eyes closed, mouth slightly open. His face presses into the curve of her chest and neck; her arms reach around him. The bronze is worked in heavy, tactile strokes — dark brown and black with green settling in every crease of muscle and hair. Highlights catch on the man's shoulder and the woman's throat; the rest sinks into shadow.

I Am Beautiful takes its title from Charles Baudelaire's poem "Her hair and her petticoat, entangled." Rodin developed the group between 1882 and 1885 from material first explored for The Gates of Hell, then released it as an independent composition. This cast was produced in 1968 at the Georges Rudier foundry in Paris under licence from the Musée Rodin, with the museum copyright and founder's inscription on the base.

Step back and the seventy-five-centimetre group reads as a single dark mass. Step in again and the intimacy returns — not a display of strength but of proximity, two bodies folded into one bronze surface.
bust-of-jean-daire:
Bust of Jean d'Aire by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Jean d'Aire, one of the six burghers of Calais, isolated in bronze — resolute, worn features that refuse heroic idealisation.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The bronze head shows an elderly man from the chest up: deeply furrowed brow, deep-set downcast eyes, thin lips set in a weary line. The surface is rough and tactile, brown patina with green in the hollows of the eyes and along the neck. Nothing here is idealised — the face is resolute, worn, and unflinching.

Jean d'Aire was one of the six burghers of Calais who offered themselves as hostages in 1347. Rodin isolated each man's psychology in the monument commissioned in 1884.

This bust was cast in December 1940 at the Alexis Rudier foundry in Paris, with the founder's mark on the exterior and a raised interior signature confirming the edition's authenticity.
seated-titan:
Seated Titan (from the Vase of the Titans) by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A single white-marble figure twisted on a rough rock — arms raised behind his head, one knee lifted, muscles straining in a compact crouch.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

One nude man sits on a block of chiselled stone, torso torqued, both arms lifted behind his head, face tilted back into shadow. A raised knee breaks the silhouette; the extended foot braces against the rock. The body is polished smooth; the base is left deliberately rough, so the contrast between finished flesh and raw stone is part of the meaning. At thirty-two centimetres the figure fits in the hand, but the stretch through the ribs and thighs reads larger.

Rodin modelled this Seated Titan around 1878–1882, soon after his return from Italy, as one of the figures he contributed to Albert-Ernest Carrier-Belleuse's Vase of the Titans. This Arkın example is an isolated white-marble rendition model, signed A. Rodin — not the full four-figure jardinière, but the same Michelangelesque crouch extracted and let stand alone.

Walk around the block. From behind the spine arches like a bow; from the side the raised knee and bowed head close into a single curve of effort. Carrier-Belleuse took the public credit for the vase; Rodin's authorship of the Titans was only formally acknowledged decades later.
titan-iv:
Titan IV (from the Vase of the Titans) (from the Vase of the Titans) by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A white-marble figure hunched on rock, arms clasped around a raised knee, head bowed — the fourth Titan, shown here as a solitary study.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The man crouches low on a rough-hewn marble block, one knee drawn up to his chest, both arms wrapped around the shin, head sunk toward the knee. The left leg hangs down the face of the stone. Muscle is modelled smoothly along the back and shoulder; the base stays jagged and unfinished. The pose is closed, inward, almost self-enclosed — less a figure supporting a weight above than one folded against his own body.

Rodin carved this Titan IV (from the Vase of the Titans) between 1878 and 1882 as part of the group he modelled for Carrier-Belleuse's Vase of the Titans, after returning from Italy. The Arkın piece is a signed white-marble rendition model at thirty-two centimetres — the single figure extracted from the decorative ensemble that Carrier signed alone.

Viewed from the side, the long curve of the spine is the whole story. From the front, only the bowed head and clasped arms are visible. It is the quietest of the four Titans, and perhaps the most modern: a body thinking, not performing.
abduction-of-hippodamia:
The Abduction of Hippodamia by Albert-Ernest Carrier-Belleuse and Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
The centaur Eurytion seizes the Lapith bride at her wedding — a violent two-handed collaboration between an established master and the young Rodin, signed in his employer's name alone.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A centaur has crashed the wedding. At the marriage feast of Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, the half-horse guests grew drunk on wine and seized the bride. The leader of the centaurs, Eurytion, lifts Hippodamia clear of the ground; her body twists away, her arm pinned against his shoulder, garlands of the wedding still scattered at his hooves. An overturned wine jar tells you everything you need to know about how the evening went.

This bronze was modelled in Carrier-Belleuse's Brussels studio between 1871 and 1879. The young Auguste Rodin had followed his master into Belgian exile after the Commune, and worked there as a praticien — a hired pair of hands. The piece is signed by Carrier alone, but scholarship since June Hargrove's research has divided the authorship: the howling, violently muscled centaur is Rodin's; the idealised, almost neoclassical bride is Carrier's. You can see the join. The two halves of the group seem to belong to two different sculptors, two different decades.

The subject — the Centauromachy, civilisation against brute appetite — was an old Greek favourite, pediment material for the Parthenon. Walk around this cast in Washington. The patina is a deep storm-green, the modelling restless. Rodin is two years away from The Age of Bronze, and already, in another man's signature, he is unmistakable.
minotaur:
The Minotaur (Faun and Nymph) by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Two bronze faces pressed together in profile — one smooth and youthful, one furrowed and gaping — intimacy and anguish caught at close range.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The sculpture fills the frame with two heads in tight contact. On the right, a young woman's face in calm profile, eyes closed, lips sealed, skin modelled smoothly. On the left, an older, ravaged face with a bulging eye and open mouth, cheek pressed against the younger one's temple. The bronze is dark and reflective, patinated to black-brown with sharp highlights along the brows, lips, and cheekbones. No bodies, no rock base in view — only this confrontation of surfaces at sixty-one centimetres.

Rodin showed the group under many titles — The Minotaur (Faun and Nymph), Faun and Nymph, Satyr and Woman — and modelled it around 1883–1885 in the midst of his work on The Gates of Hell. This Arkın cast was produced in 2013 at the Susse foundry in Paris, signed and stamped EA III/IV, with a rich brown and green patina.

Walk around the pair and the reading shifts with every angle: from one side the smooth profile dominates; from the other, the gaping mouth and staring eye take over. Rodin compresses an entire drama into the narrow space between two cheeks.
camille-claudel-bonnet:
Bust of Camille Claudel Wearing a Bonnet by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A young woman's bronze head under a loosely modelled bonnet — eyes lowered, mouth set, the face worked with Rodin's quick, searching touch.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The bonnet sits high on the crown, modelled in rough, sketch-like strokes that contrast with the smoother planes of the face. The eyes are open but cast downward; the long straight nose and closed mouth hold a pensive stillness. The neck ends in a jagged cut on a square wooden block. Dark brown patina with green in the recesses catches light along the cheekbones and the ridge of the bonnet.

This is Camille Claudel, around 1884, modelled by her lover and teacher at the very beginning of the most consuming relationship in either of their lives.

Camille came to Rodin's studio in 1883 as a pupil, not yet twenty. He was forty-three, in his first full bloom of fame. Within a year she was his collaborator, his model, his muse and — soon — his mistress. He sculpted her many times over the decade that followed: as La Pensée, as the head of Aurora, as the goddess of dawn breaking through marble. This early head, known as Camille au bonnet, is the most direct of those portraits, the closest to private observation.

Walk slowly around it. There is no performance here, no allegory. Rodin has caught the inwardness of a young, brilliant, formidably difficult woman thinking. The lowered gaze and the contrast between rough cap and finely polished face are pure Rodin — a way of saying the work is unfinished because the sitter is unfinished, still becoming. Within ten years Camille would break with him. The bonnet remains.
mme-rodin:
Mask of Rose Beuret by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
The face of Rose Beuret — Rodin's companion for fifty-three years — modelled as a mask with closed eyes, softened deliberately to avoid the casting-from-life scandal that had haunted him since 1877.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The eyes are closed and the face has been left to read like a mask, lifted from a body that is no longer there. This is the woman who shared Rodin's life for fifty-three years: Marie-Rose Beuret, a seamstress from the Lorraine countryside who met him in 1864 when she was twenty, bore his only son, kept his studio while he was unknown, and married him only weeks before they both died in 1917.

Rodin first modelled her around 1880 as the fierce, helmeted Bellona. By the time of this portrait, conceived around 1882, the look is different — quieter, withdrawn, the features blurred deliberately to skirt the scandal that had nearly ended his career when critics accused him of casting The Age of Bronze directly from life. He kept her bust slightly smaller than life-size, the surfaces left soft, the hair barely indicated. Nothing here invites accusation. Everything here invites looking.

Stand close. You can see the long history of the relationship in the modelling — the affection, the inattention, the late, slightly guilty tenderness of a man who took her devotion as a fact of his daily existence. Cast by Alexis Rudier in bronze, the head is also known as the Mask of Madame Rodin. It is Rose without performance, as the studio knew her: silent, lowered, indispensable.
mask-of-hanako:
Mask of Hanako, Study Type E by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A small bronze mask of Hanako — open eyes, closed lips, the face calm and mask-like on a veined stone pedestal.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The face is modelled frontally with East Asian features: broad nose, full closed lips, almond-shaped eyes open and level. The back and crown of the head are left rough, as if torn from a larger block. Dark brown patina warms the cheeks; reddish tones gather in the hollows. The mask sits on a square pedestal with a crackled stone texture. At seventeen point eight centimetres it is a portrait reduced to its essentials.

This is Hanako — born Ohta Hisa in 1868, the Japanese actress who became one of Rodin's most obsessively studied sitters during the last decade of his life. He made fifty-eight heads of her between 1907 and 1911, more than of any other model.

Rodin first saw Hanako perform in Marseille in 1906, in a touring company managed by the American dancer Loïe Fuller. Her plays were Westernised pastiches of Japanese theatre, written for European audiences and culminating, almost always, in a bloody scene of ritual suicide. It was Hanako's face in that moment of extreme anguish — taut, drained, transcendent — that struck Rodin. He brought her to Meudon and asked her to hold her death-scene expressions while he modelled.

This is Étude Type E, one of the variations Rodin made in 1907. The Victoria & Albert Museum holds a remarkable version cast in pâte de verre by Jean Cros in 1912 — Hanako in coloured glass, almost translucent at the temples. The mask shown here is the bronze. Stand close. Even at rest she seems to be listening for something just out of frame. Rodin would later say that her face contained all the expressive power of a Roman bust by Donatello. Hanako, he thought, was a sculpture before he touched her.
head-of-lust:
Head of Lust by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A man's bronze head bowed low — brow heavy, eyes in shadow, mouth slightly parted, grief worked into every lump of surface.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The head tilts down and turns slightly to one side. Deep brows shadow the eyes; the lips part just enough to suggest breath or speech withheld. Thick, wavy hair is modelled in rough masses; the neck is muscular, cut off at the chest in a jagged truncation. The bronze is glossy dark brown and green-black, highlights running along the forehead, nose, and cheekbone while the eyes stay in darkness.

Rodin conceived Head of Lust in 1882 for The Gates of Hell, where a female figure of Lust appears in the group Avarice and Lust. This Arkın cast was produced by Alexis Rudier between 1917 and 1918, with the founder's mark on the base and a repeat interior signature. At thirty-seven point three centimetres it reads as an isolated study head — heavy, inward, resistant to quick reading.

Stand close and the downward tilt becomes the whole subject. From above you see the crown of the head and the set of the shoulders; from below, the open mouth and the weight of the brow. Rodin leaves you to decide whether this is sorrow, exhaustion, or something held back.
mask-broken-nose:
Mask of the Man with the Broken Nose by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
The bearded, battered face of a Paris handyman known only as Bibi — modelled by the 23-year-old Rodin in a freezing studio, refused twice by the Salon, and remembered by Rodin as his first real work.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A bearded face, scarred, broken-nosed, neither young nor classically beautiful. Rodin would later call this his first real work — “the first piece of modelling I ever did.” He was twenty-three.

The sitter was a local odd-job man known only as Bibi, who lived near Rodin's freezing Saint-Marcel studio in 1863. Rodin worked on the head for over a year. One winter night the studio's heating failed, the clay froze, and the back of the head simply broke off. He kept the fragment and called it a mask. He submitted it to the Salon des Beaux-Arts in 1864; it was refused. He submitted it again in 1865; refused again. The jurors thought it unfinished. They were not yet ready for a portrait of an ageing labourer with a broken nose, modelled as carefully as a Roman emperor.

Stand close. The features are utterly naturalistic, but the hair is treated like the curls of a late Hellenistic bust, the blank eyes like classical sculpture. Rodin was already doing what he would do for the next fifty years — pulling the language of antiquity down into the bodies of ordinary, unflattering, particular people. The mask was finally accepted in 1875 and cast in bronze. Bibi, who never knew his sitter's name was about to become art history, had been Rodin's first true subject.
torso-great-shadow:
Torso of the Great Shadow by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
An enlarged, headless and armless torso drawn out of The Gates of Hell, where it once stood as one of the Three Shades pointing down to Dante's inscription.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Stand close and the eye starts upward, then catches: there is no head to meet. The body arches as if straining against a weight pressed down through invisible shoulders, the chest pulled open, the abdomen drawn tight. Without arms to balance it, the torso seems to answer only to gravity and to itself — a fragment turned, paradoxically, into a whole.

Rodin first modelled the figure as one of the Three Shades crowning The Gates of Hell. Each of those mournful sentries leans inward, hand falling toward Dante's inscription — Lasciate ogni speranza, voi ch'entrate. Around 1900, working with his enlarger Henri Lebossé, Rodin had the headless, armless core of the Shade scaled up beyond life size. Lebossé, awed by what came out of the studio, called it perhaps the most important piece of sculpture of Rodin's career.

The kinship with the antique Belvedere Torso — Michelangelo's lodestar — is deliberate. Rodin had long argued that a fragment could carry more truth than a finished figure, that incompleteness was a form of intensity. Walk around the bronze slowly: every angle gives you a different drama of muscle and shadow, but no resolution. That is the point. The Great Shadow keeps its head and its arms to itself.
head-jean-de-fiennes:
Head of Jean de Fiennes by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A bronze head thrown sharply backward — mouth open, eyes sunk in shadow, anguish concentrated in a face without a body.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Only the head survives, mounted on a two-tier black pedestal. It tilts back and slightly to one side, mouth parted, eyes hollowed into darkness. The modelling is rough and urgent — hair in thick clumps, skin lumpy with tool marks, highlights catching on the forehead and cheekbone while the sockets stay black. There is no torso, no drapery, no outstretched arms — just this isolated face at thirty-two point two centimetres.

Jean de Fiennes was the youngest of the six burghers of Calais who offered themselves as hostages in 1347. Rodin received the monument commission in 1884 and modelled each citizen as a separate psychological study. This head was conceived in 1886; the Arkın cast was made in 1984 at the Émile Godard foundry under Musée Rodin licence.

Stand low and the backward throw reads as defiance; stand high and it reads as surrender. Rodin gives you a single angle of a young man's fear and lets the rest go unstated.
head-pierre-de-wiessant:
Head of Pierre de Wissant by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
An over-life-size head of one of the Burghers of Calais, frozen in the long instant of fear — eyes hollow, mouth half-open, surface still bearing Rodin's working marks.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Pierre de Wissant was one of the six wealthy citizens of Calais who, in 1347, offered themselves to Edward III of England as hostages so the besieged town might be spared. Rodin, modelling his monument five centuries later, refused the patriotic cliché and instead pulled each man down into private terror. This is Pierre's face enlarged beyond life, as if the sculptor wanted you to read the smallest shift of mouth and eyelid as you would on a stage.

Look at the surface. Rodin worked the plaster directly — graphite lines flicker through the temple, washes of tint sink into the hollows beneath the eyes, the skin still bears the press of his fingers. Nothing is smoothed or polished. The head is unfinished in the academic sense and finished in every other.

He exhibited the life-size figure of Pierre alone, separately from the monument group, while still working on the ensemble — convinced that each burgher carried a complete drama. Stand in front of this head and you understand why. The mouth is just open; some word has been thought but not said. Walk slowly to the side and the whole face seems to sink another fraction. That fraction is the entire subject.
head-eustache-de-saint-pierre:
Head of Eustache de Saint-Pierre by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
The bearded, hollow-eyed head of the eldest burgher — the man who, by all the chronicles, was first to volunteer his life for Calais.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A bearded bronze head faces forward: deep furrows across the brow, hollow eyes, thick mustache and bushy beard with green patina settled in the recesses. The face is gaunt, weathered, sorrowful — mounted on a metal post above a wooden two-tier base. At thirty-five centimetres it reads as a portrait stripped to essentials.

Eustache de Saint-Pierre was the eldest of the six citizens of Calais who, in 1347, walked out of the besieged city in shirts, with ropes about their necks, to surrender themselves to Edward III. The chronicles single him out as the first to step forward.

Rodin modelled Eustache in 1886 from the painter Jean-Charles Cazin, a native of the Pas-de-Calais whose features he thought carried the right inheritance. He did not give the burgher heroic posture. The cheekbones sharpen against the temples; the mouth is set but tired; the brow leans slightly forward, as though the head has already begun the walk it cannot refuse.

Stand to one side and the brow catches the light first — the cheekbones sharpen, the mouth sets, the eyes sink deeper into shadow. Isolated from the full figure, the head becomes an essay on what it costs a man to give himself away.
eve-small-model:
Eve, small model by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A small-scale Eve who has folded herself into her own shame — arms wrapped across her face and body, head sunk into the shadow she has made of her arms.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Rodin began Eve in 1881 as a pendant to Adam, both intended to flank the Gates of Hell. He worked from an Italian model, one of the Abruzzesi sisters, and noticed early on that her body was changing — without telling him, she was pregnant. The figure he ended up modelling carries that secret weight: a thickness through the abdomen, a thigh that no longer quite agrees with itself, a body just beginning to lean inward against what it cannot any longer hide.

The small model — the petit modèle, with its square base and flat feet — was finished and shown by 1883. Around forty bronze casts were eventually pulled, by François Rudier, Griffoul & Lorge, Perzinka, Alexis Rudier and finally Georges Rudier as late as 1967. The first owners loved it because it brought the monumental Eve down into a domestic room without losing any of the moral force.

Rilke described her best: "Eve stands with head sunk deeply into the shadow of the arms." Approach her quietly. The arms close over the breasts and the face; the shoulders curve forward; the body has already begun its long walk out of paradise. You are looking at the moment just after the apple.
meditation:
Meditation, or The Inner Voice by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A turning, twisting figure conceived for the abandoned Pantheon monument to Victor Hugo — afterwards drawn out as a work of its own, often shown without arms.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A standing nude woman twists in an S-curve: head bowed against her folded right arm, left arm raised, legs crossed at the thigh, right foot planted on a rocky bronze base. The surface is dark brown, hand-modelled, muscles picking up light along the hip and ribcage. She seems to be listening to something inside her own chest.

Meditation, or The Inner Voice began as a Muse on Rodin's abandoned monument to Victor Hugo for the Panthéon, conceived in 1885.

The Panthéon plan collapsed and Rodin, refusing to lose the figure, lifted her out of the group. In 1896 he had her enlarged to almost life size. She turns. The hip throws out, the chest rotates against the shoulders, the head sinks toward the further breast — a whole body listening inward. In many casts she has no arms; in some, no legs below the knee. Rodin was unrepentant. "My statues without arms," he told Rilke, "lack nothing essential to them."

Alexis Rudier cast thirteen examples between 1921 and 1943; the master plaster remains at the Musée Rodin in Meudon, and other casts live in Stockholm, Tokyo, London. Stand still in front of her. The figure does not pose for you. She is mid-sentence inside her own head, and the bronze is the only thing thick enough to hold what she is hearing.
triumphant-youth:
Triumphant Youth by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A man and woman locked in a bronze kiss on a rocky base — her head thrown back, his arm around her, the group glowing with golden-brown patina.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A nude man sits on rough rock, leaning back as a woman drapes across his lap. Her right arm reaches around his neck; his hand rests on her thigh. Their lips meet at the centre of the composition. The bronze carries a rich golden-brown patina, darker in the crevices of the rock and the folds between their bodies. Musculature is modelled with Rodin's characteristic blend of polish and roughness — smooth along the woman's arched back, restless in the stone beneath them.

Rodin showed this group as Triumphant Youth at the 1896 Paris Salon, though he also exhibited it under other titles — Eternal Youth, The Grandmother's Kiss, Old Age and Adolescence. It was conceived in 1894. This Arkın cast bears the Thiébault Frères foundry inscription and stands at fifty-two centimetres.

Walk around the base and the embrace keeps rearranging itself: from behind, the man's broad back; from the front, the woman's thrown-back head; from the side, the narrow bridge of the kiss. Rodin gave the group many names because it refuses to settle into one story.
iris-study-with-head:
Iris, Study with Head by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A headless bronze figure balanced on one leg, the other kicked out sideways, one arm gone at the shoulder — acrobatic strain frozen in dark patinated metal.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The figure stands on a bent right leg, left leg extended horizontally. The head is absent — a rough stump at the neck — and the left arm ends at the shoulder. The right arm reaches across the torso to grasp the extended foot. Muscles torque through the abdomen and thigh; the surface is dark brown-green, highlights running along the chest and the outstretched limb. At fifty-three centimetres the pose reads as a single line of tension from foot to hip to stump.

Rodin conceived Iris, messagère des dieux between 1890 and 1891, originally for his Monument to Victor Hugo. He later removed the head and arm from many versions, leaving the headless, splayed figure that became one of his most discussed works. This Arkın cast was produced by Susse Fondeurs for the Musée Rodin between 1969 and 1972.

Walk around the figure and the balance keeps shifting — from the front the reaching arm pulls the eye across the body; from the side the horizontal leg shoots outward like a lever. What looks like flight is held together only by the standing foot.
falling-man:
The Falling Man by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A figure of the damned hurled backwards over the lintel of The Gates of Hell, twisting away from a force that cannot be resisted.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Among the writhing crowd Rodin pinned to The Gates of Hell, the Falling Man holds a particular position: he is the figure who escapes nothing. Conceived in the early 1880s as Rodin laboured on the great portal, he was placed in the upper left of the doors, half straddling the lintel that separates the tympanum from the panels below. He has begun to topple backwards, and the bronze captures exactly the instant before the fall becomes irreversible.

No casts of the figure were made during Rodin's lifetime. The Susse foundry pulled twelve bronzes for the Musée Rodin between 1972 and 1982, and this is one of them. As a free-standing piece, away from the Gate, the Falling Man reveals what is masked when he is welded into the swarm — the deep curve of his back, the great forward push of the chest, the head thrown over the right shoulder as though already glimpsing what is rushing up to meet him.

Walk around him slowly. The composition has no rest point. Every line — arm, ribcage, thigh — leans against another. Rodin once said he wanted his figures to express, in the body, what the face could not. Here is the body in unanswered prayer.
monumental-torso:
Monumental Torso by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
An enlarged, headless and armless torso drawn out of the Falling Man — a fragment scaled up until it stands alone, beyond rescue and beyond escape.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

By 1904, Rodin had spent twenty years pulling figures off and on the great relief of The Gates of Hell, working them up at new scales, refusing to let them stay anonymous in the swarm. The Monumental Torso is one of these salvages. It begins with the Falling Man — the writhing figure half-toppled over the upper left lintel of the Gate — and ends as a thing entirely its own: head gone, arms cut at the shoulder, legs ending mid-thigh.

The figure was never cast in Rodin's lifetime. In 1970, the Georges Rudier foundry pulled this version on commission from the Musée Rodin, at just over a metre high. The torso retains every push of Rodin's thumb. Look at the way the chest opens to the sky, ribs arcing under the skin, the abdomen still tensed against a fall already begun. Without the limbs to give the action a direction, the body becomes a piece of pure pressure.

Rodin had argued since his youth that a fragment, properly chosen, could carry more truth than a complete figure. Walk slowly around this one and the case makes itself. There is nowhere for the eye to settle: every angle gives a different drama of muscle and shadow, and none resolves.
eternal-spring-first-state:
Eternal Spring, First State by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Rodin's earliest conception of Eternal Spring — a young man bent backwards over a rock, drawing a girl across his lap into a kiss. For most connoisseurs, the finest of all the variants.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

A man leans back against rough rock, one arm flung out horizontally; a woman arches across his lap, head thrown back to meet his kiss. Their bodies emerge from a heavily textured craggy base, dark brown-green patina highlighting the smooth skin of the lovers against the restless stone.

L'Éternel Printemps was conceived in 1884 alongside The Kiss, originally intended for The Gates of Hell before Rodin released it as an independent composition.

What makes the Premier État rare and prized is its rawness. There are only five bronze casts of this earliest version: two pulled by Alexis Rudier between 1930 and 1952, and three more by Georges Rudier between 1966 and 1969. The Musée Rodin's contract list ends with the present example. In later states, Rodin and his collaborators softened the composition, but here the young man is still bent extravagantly backwards over the rock, and the girl is still flung across him — knees splayed, hair loose, the whole body offering itself.

Stand close. The lovers' faces have not quite met. Eternal Spring went on to become one of Rodin's most commercially successful icons of romance, and yet this — the first state — still feels as if the couple had only met that morning.
the-kiss-3rd-reduction:
The Kiss, 3rd Reduction by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A small-scale, chamber version of Rodin's most famous embrace — Paolo and Francesca caught in the kiss that, in Dante, will cost them eternity.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

At chamber scale, a man leans over a woman seated on rock; her head angles up to meet his lips, his arm across her shoulder, her arm around his neck. Dark lustrous patina runs brown and black with green in the hair and the hollows of the shoulders. The embrace is tight, quiet, almost entirely upper body.

The couple began on The Gates of Hell as Paolo and Francesca da Rimini from Dante's Inferno, before Rodin lifted them out as an independent work.

Le Baiser as a free-standing work was exhibited in plaster in Brussels in 1887 and in bronze in Paris later the same year. In 1898 Rodin signed a ten-year contract with the Barbedienne foundry to cast an unlimited edition in four reduced scales — 72 cm, 60 cm, 40 cm and 25 cm. The 3ème Réduction at 39.5 cm corresponds to the third of those sizes and was cast in considerable numbers between 1910 and 1918.

What survives the reduction is the quiet of the gesture. Francesca leans into Paolo; their lips meet; his book, which Dante mentions, lies forgotten on the rock at her hip. Approach close and you can read the pulse of the moment. They do not yet know it cannot last.
death-of-adonis:
Death of Adonis by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
Adonis, the young god of beauty mortally wounded by a wild boar, lies across the body of Aphrodite — a compact, intensely felt elegy that began life as a marginal sketch beside one of Baudelaire's poems.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

The group is not large — barely the size of a forearm — but Rodin has charged it with the gravity of a tomb. Adonis is dead. He lies face down across the body of Aphrodite, who half kneels, half collapses beneath him, holding what is left of him as if she could still warm him back. The two bodies are wrapped so tightly into one mass that, walking around the bronze, you sometimes lose track of where one figure ends and the other begins.

Rodin first sketched the composition in 1887 in the margin of Baudelaire's poem Le Poison, inside a copy of Les Fleurs du Mal that the publisher Paul Gallimard had asked him to illustrate. He exhibited the sculpture under three different titles in three different cities — Venus and Adonis in Brussels, Hero and Leander in London, and finally Death of Adonis — the same group of mourning lovers re-named each time after another mythical death.

The figure of Adonis is in fact recycled from The Gates of Hell, where she appears, female, on the upper lintel as part of Man and his Thought. Rodin liked to swap his figures' sexes and stories freely; what matters is the posture. Lean close: the curve of the back, the slack hand, the way Aphrodite presses her cheek into his shoulder. You are watching the precise moment when desire becomes grief.
jardiniere-of-the-titans:
The Titans' Jardinière by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A plain terracotta bowl borne by four straining nude figures — matte, unglazed, every surface showing the press of hands and tools.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Four muscular men crouch around a central support, shoulders and raised arms bearing a shallow dish above their heads. The material is light beige terracotta, unglazed, with visible fingerprints and tool marks across the bodies and the bowl. Drapery winds between the figures and the central column. One man hunches forward with head down; another reaches a flat palm up into the bowl. The whole piece sits on a tall dark wooden pedestal.

Rodin modelled the figures around 1877 while working for Albert Carrier-Belleuse, who designed the vessel and signed the jardinière. This Arkın example is terracotta at thirty-nine point one centimetres, signed A. Carrier Belleuse — an unglazed cast rather than the polychrome glazed versions in Paris, Cleveland, or Detroit.

Walk around the base and each Titan offers a different angle of strain — bent back, raised arm, tucked head. The bowl is plain; the drama is entirely in the bodies beneath it.
eternal-idol-small-model:
Eternal Idol, Small Model by Auguste Rodin, French, 1840 to 1917.

<break time="1.2s" />
A man kneels with his hands locked behind his back and presses his lips to a standing woman's breast — Rodin's most intense small group of adoration, mistrust, and worship, modelled while The Gates of Hell were still in his studio.

<break time="1.2s" />
About the work.

Rodin made the group in 1889 while still wrestling with The Gates of Hell. Both figures began separately on the right-hand door before he pulled them out and pressed them together. The man kneels, his hands fastened behind his back as though tied. The woman stands above him, one leg drawn up, looking down with a face that is almost without expression. He buries his mouth in her breast in what could be a prayer, an act of surrender, or a confession he cannot say aloud.

Rodin gave it three different titles during his lifetime. He called it L'Hostie — the Host — invoking the wafer at communion. He called it Le Sacrifice. He finally settled on L'Éternelle Idole. The titles agree on one thing: the woman is divine, and the man, however abject, is also somehow free to worship.

The first cast of this 17-centimetre version, in 1891, went to the collector Antoni Roux. Roux pushed Rodin to enlarge it, and a marble was carved by Jean Escoula in 1893. But the small bronze keeps something the larger versions soften. The composition is closed and concentrated, the size of a held thing. The novelist Rainer Maria Rilke, who briefly served as Rodin's secretary, said of it: 'Heaven is near, but has not yet been reached; Hell is near, but has not yet been forgotten.' Look at the man's hands. They are not quite bound, and not quite free.
